back: Chickens in the system: controlling insects/pests, enriching soil and food

Chickens can help on an empty bed after harvesting. They scratch among crop residue and eat some insects and weed seed. Their manure and bedding can be composted and returned to the soil. Foraging does not take the place of properly nutritious feed, clean water, shelter and daily care.

A chicken tractor is a moving coop without a floor (a chicken coop that can be moved). Move it before the ground has no plants, becomes mud, or is covered too heavily by manure. The right time depends on the chickens, soil and weather. No single number of chickens guarantees there will be enough soil enrichment across the whole site.

Keep chickens away from seedlings and from crops harvested for food. Fresh manure can carry germs. Ask an agricultural adviser to tell you how to handle manure safely before planting the next crop. Ducks scratch less, but may still damage plants and turn wet soil into mud. Watch the birds and move them when necessary.

back:
Honeybees and other insects carry flower pollen and drop it on other flowers. This helps many fruit and vegetable crops, including avocado. Crops and varieties differ in what they need for pollination. A hive does not guarantee a better harvest everywhere: weather, water, plant health and other pollinating insects also matter.

South Africa has two other small types (subspecies) of native honeybees. The Cape honeybee is found in the Western Cape and some parts of the Eastern Cape. The African honeybee is native to central Africa and most of Southern Africa. These natural areas, in general, are not a guide for moving bees. The Department's control measures set a dividing line for bee movement. Check the current rules for moving bees with the Department and an experienced local beekeeper before moving bees or hives.

Learn from an experienced local beekeeper before getting a hive. Keep hives away from busy paths, homes and places where children play. Morning sun can help; a safe site matters first. Give bees flowering plants through all seasons and avoid exposing bees to pesticides. Active bees are not proof that a farm has no chemicals or diseases. National honeybee control measures require registration for specified beekeeping activities, including managed hives for bee products, queen rearing, commercial pollination, and removal, destruction or moving of a colony. Ask the Department if you are not sure whether the rules apply to your activity. If a colony repeatedly swarms, ask a trained beekeeper to inspect it. Crowding is one possible reason, not a diagnosis.

Integrating livestock cycles: nutrients that move around the farm

Some nutrients can return to the planting area in compost made with manure. Fresh manure can carry harmful germs. Fully compost manure before using it near food crops. Bought feed brings nutrients into the farm, while food and other products remove them. Keep a record of bought feed and food sold or taken for the home. Food scraps alone may not meet the animals' needs.

Guinea fowl forage for insects and may eat ticks (small blood-sucking creatures). Do not trust them to protect people or livestock from ticks or tick-borne diseases. Inspect the animals and follow the local animal health plan.

For each animal, ask: what can it eat here? What useful things does it produce? What else does it need? Combine water, suitable feed, shelter, fencing and daily care.

Chickens following goats is not a proven way to replace goat worm control. Grazing management can help, but goats still need health checks and a parasite plan (organisms living on others) from a vet or animal health adviser. Do not stop treatment because chickens visited the grazing camp.

Build living soil with compost, mulch, cover crops and worm farms
A soil cross-section shows dark topsoil above pale subsoil, with two worms. Beside it, a soil jar settles into three layers — sand, silt and clay.
Understanding your soil: the foundation of everything

Soil contains many kinds of living things. Bacteria and fungi help decompose organic matter (decaying material from plants and animals) and cycle nutrients.

Some fungi help roots get nutrients. Worm channels can help water and air enter the soil.

Look at roots, soil structure and water movement, and visible soil life.

Put soil and water in a clear jar, with a little suitable detergent for separating soil particles (dispersing detergent). Close it, shake it, then leave it undisturbed.

Sand settles first. Silt (soil finer than sand) follows, while clay can stay suspended in the water for a very long time.

This is a simple learning test. Clumps and unsettled clay can mislead you; use a soil lab when you need texture to be accurate.

A firm sand layer under cloudy water does not yet tell you the final proportion. Some fine particles may still be suspended in the water.

Compare the settled layers and test the soil by hand in the field.

Write down what you see and everything still uncertain. Do not decide irrigation or soil treatment based on one jar alone.

Compaction, poor drainage and loss of organic matter can reduce roots and soil life.

Pale colour or few worms do not prove that chemicals killed the soil. Worm activity changes with moisture and season.

Look at patterns across the whole field. Check management history, drainage and crop growth before choosing a treatment.

back: Making and using compost

Compost is organic matter decomposed under controlled conditions.

Finished compost can improve soil structure and contributes nutrients.

Time to readiness varies with materials, moisture, air and temperature. A province name or a fixed number of weeks is not a readiness test.

Mix dry browns (dry brown materials) with fresh greens (fresh green materials). Avoid thick, wet layers that block air.

If the heap becomes slimy or smells strongly of ammonia, add dry browns and turn it.

Check moisture and air as the heap changes; one recipe does not suit all mixtures of materials.

A hot middle temperature does not guarantee every part of the heap has been treated. Time, temperature and management all matter.

Do not put meat, milk and dairy products, diseased plants, pet waste and contaminated materials in this simple home process.

Do not assume home composting destroys all weed seed or all disease-causing organisms. Use a recognised process where sanitisation is needed.

Do not put wattle seed BAGS/SACKS into the compost heap. An ordinary heap may not make all the seed unable to grow.

Use only clean, untreated materials. Tree bark decomposes slowly; being only bark does not guarantee it cannot be contaminated.

Check the heap and turn it when it needs air or more mixing. Keep it moist rather than waterlogged.

back: Covering the soil and cover crops: protecting and building soil

Cover bare soil with suitable, clean mulch, such as straw, dry grass or wood chips.

Mulch can reduce water loss by evaporation, soften rain impact and suppress weeds.

Keep it away from tree and plant stems. Check moisture underneath and adjust the layer; more mulch is not always better.

Cover crops can protect soil between main crops. Choose by local climate, available water and the next planting.

Course examples include oats, lupins, sunn hemp and cowpea. Check local suitability before sowing.

Legumes (plants like beans) need the right bacteria and growing conditions to fix nitrogen. Nutrients in their residue become available as the material decomposes.

Worm farms can turn suitable food scraps and bedding into worm castings. Check the bin rather than expecting a fixed harvest date.

The liquid that drips naturally from a worm bin is called leachate. It is not the same as prepared worm-castings tea.

Leachate can contain harmful organisms or harmful substances. Do not use it on edible crops or assume that diluting it with water makes it safe.

A Highveld field left bare after the maize harvest faces two main risks.

Winter wind can carry away dry topsoil.

The first big spring storm can hit bare soil and damage its surface and structure. If water runs across the field, it can carry loose soil.

Cover crops, mulch and organic matter can help hold soil in place and keep it alive.
